utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We move to a new witness. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It will be Mr. Slobodan Vukovic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vukovic. Welcome to the Tribunal. If you would be kind enough to take the affirmation which is on the card now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to sit down. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vukovic. What is your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you live in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you lived in Dubrovnik for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Practically since I was born, although I was born in Mostar, I lived in Mostar only for one month. I spent my entire life in that town except for my university studies from 1971 until 1979 when I studied and worked in Zagreb at the school of architecture of the University of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So your period in Dubrovnik, we're talking a little over a half a century?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you studied architecture in Zagreb. Did you graduate with a degree of bachelor of architecture?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you studying for a masters degree in architecture?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the entire coursework involved in the masters degree at the university. And I am working on the masters degree itself, a paper entitled "The Design of gardens and landscaping" with Dubrovnik as an example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of the Croatian Association of Architects?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a member of the Croatian Chamber of Architects and Civil Engineers which was established only at the beginning of 2000, and I am a member of the Association of Croatian Architects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the professional bodies that license architects in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Chamber of Architects gives permits to engage in this particular line of work in Croatia. And without this license, no one can be involved in this profession. This started in 1999, and it is still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, was there a formal system of accreditation of architects in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a state examination that was supposed to be passed, and then you would get a certificate. You had to pass a special professional examination. You would get this certificate, and this certificate meant that you could professionally work on town planning and other architectural work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work after you completed your studies in 1979?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My practice started at the faculty of architecture itself. I worked there on particular projects, specifically the project of the restoration of the music school in Dubrovnik. I did that within a project of restoration, rather projects of restoration that followed after the earthquake of Dubrovnik from 1979.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you do your JNA military service?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did my military service from 1980 to 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left your military service, where did you work and what was your job?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I spent some time in Zagreb working on the same project very briefly. And after that, in 1981, in the summer of 1981, I returned to Dubrovnik, and I got a job in the town planning service, or rather the Institute for the Construction of Dubrovnik had a sector that was involved in town planning, the town planning of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that office attached to the Dubrovnik Municipality, that is, the local council?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only office in the territory of the former Municipality of Dubrovnik that was involve in town planning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your job title an architect within that office?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was my job title.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become a lead architect within that office, or a leading architect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After a few years of working there, I later became the leader of certain projects that were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to briefly tell the Trial Chamber what sort of work you did in that office between 1981 and 1991, if you could just list the sorts of things you did.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My activity primarily had to do with town planning. Town planning consisted of a particular method that required familiarity with the existing situation, and then, after having analysed the existing situation, it was necessary to prepare documentation for conservation projects. Since this is an area that has many cultural monuments, even outside the nucleus of the Old Town. Town planning was based on this analysis and an assessment as to what can be done, so basically, it consisted of designing new parts of town. Actually, this was the primary activity that we were involved in. In addition to that, we worked on architectural projects, but that was not a major portion of our work. Specifically then, I worked in Cavtat on the reconstruction of two facilities. That was actually an adaptation of an old school building. It was being turned into an apartment building. And the methodology that was applied there was later applied in the reconstruction of other monuments within Dubrovnik and within the Old Town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your work involve zoning issues?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your question properly, it meant, of course, within our methodology that certain areas should be zoned. So this was the so-called zoning plan. And it was specified what kind of construction would take place within such zones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it involve the assessment of heritage values of property in the Dubrovnik Municipality, and in particular, the UNESCO-protected Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, I did not work directly on planning within the Old Town nucleus, but my colleagues did. So we exchanged information and knowledge in terms of how to respond to certain challenges, like what was supposed to be done within the Old Town nucleus itself. So I'm talking about the Old Town of Dubrovnik within the city walls. It was customary that for every plan, preliminary documentation would be planned, the so-called conservation documentation, regardless of whether it was within the Old Town nucleus or outside it, and then the number of buildings would be specified as well as the area around the buildings that should particularly be reviewed and how the entire matter should be resolved in view of the exceptional historical importance of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as of December 1991, what experience did you have in building inspection, measuring buildings, and urban spaces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My experience in relation to what you mentioned in your question is part of our elementary professional training. Since the area of Dubrovnik and Croatia has an enormous number of cultural monuments, when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we had staff meetings at university, we had special courses related to this particular subject matter; that is to say, dealing with heritage. So we actually did master this method of identifying existing buildings and adjacent areas which involved measurement and presenting what we saw through architectural drawing and design. That was one part of the exercise involved. The other one was actually a method of diagnosis which was supposed to identify the actual state that the building was in from the point of view of construction and from the point of view of its functionality. Then we would actually engage in prognosis which meant we would decide what should be done within the building involved. So this is the experience I got at university staff meetings. And also, through my graduate studies, I received additional training and preparation in terms of heritage and monuments as such. This was a particular field of interest for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about on-the-job experience of the things you just outlined when you were working for the Dubrovnik Municipality? Did you do those sorts of things up until 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that my basic activity was town planning. This had to do with individual buildings that in a way evolved along parallel lines with town planning itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever lived in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is my town. I'm actually a child of that town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe your familiarity with the Old Town and the buildings and objects within it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I am very familiar with it. I had accumulated all of that from a material and spiritual point of view, and it actually formed my personality, living in the Old Town. I was always very proud of that. I am very proud of that. And I shall always be very proud of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you move from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Zagreb and when I started working. That was in 1981. However, my mother stayed in the Old Town at the place where I grew up and where I graduated from high school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is that place in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Buniceva Poljana. It is a square by the cathedral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you living in the second half of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in Lapad, Put Vojnovica 104.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your mother still living in the Old Town in the second half of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you go to the Old Town and visit your mother in September, October, November and the first half of December 1991? When I say how often, how regularly would you go and visit her?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't that I went regularly since I spent most of my time in Lapad where my office was and in a way it was in a special situation. Because of the situation at the time, it was our official duty to stay in the office and to take good care of the maps and everything else we had. So I went once or twice a week. However, I spoke to her on the telephone very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When do you remember the shelling commencing in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I well remember that moment. I even remember the day and hour. Towards the end of September at a meeting of the executive council of the Municipality of Dubrovnik. I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just more interested in the date rather than the full details of your experience.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the end of September or the beginning of October, roughly. I can't remember exactly. But I think that it was the last day of September or the first day of October, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just very briefly, what was your experience of shelling the Dubrovnik area in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was shocking. It was a shocking experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times was the area shelled or how often?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, because after all it has been 13 years, I cannot recall each and every detail, at first I actually noticed and we all noticed jets flying over Dubrovnik at a low altitude. And this was a signal as far as we were concerned that there was something unpleasant in store for the entire town. After that, bombardment followed. Not very frequently and in all fairness outside the Old Town nucleus. It was not very frequent, but then the intensity increased, as far as I can remember, as time went by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The jets flying over Dubrovnik, could you identify which army they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any pattern to the bombardment as it's described in the translation over October-November 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say. I'm simply not in a position now to say anything in terms of whether a pattern existed or not. Except for what I said before, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about frequency? Can you say anything about your impression now of the frequency of it during that period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I know that close to the reporting centre that had been directly bombed, this is a facility near the hospital. That was intensive bombing. So basically, my daughter who was two years old at the time experienced a shock. She could not recover for a long time from this sound of aircraft. And actually she felt insecure whenever she would hear the sound of any kind of airplane after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your -- you just mentioned your daughter. Did your wife and daughter remain in Dubrovnik during the second half of 1991? Or did they leave?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: After the dangers that increased every day in terms of living in the town, refugees got organised and started leaving on ships, mainly women and children. My wife and daughter thus left on a ship called Marina from Gruz harbour towards Split where my wife's mother lives and further on where my wife had more family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue working throughout the period of October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We did not work. Our only concern was to take care of our documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little while back, you mentioned or were mentioning something I think you called the executive council. Was that a body attached to the Dubrovnik Municipality for which you were working?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not work on the executive council, but I worked in the Institute for Territorial Planning and Environment Protection which was a technical service of the municipality dealing with plans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what the executive council was within the Dubrovnik Municipality, what its function was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the municipality, it was actually a local government, the city government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about executive board or executive council? Do you know what its function was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The function of the executive council in terms of my line of work was to approve, endorse certain designs and forward them to the assembly for approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In October-November 1991, was that body, the executive council, a civilian body attached to the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I no longer had any insight into things after that last meeting which was the last occasion when I saw all the members of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was the Old Town shelled in October or November 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about shelling of the Old Town in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was out of town, I had received information about something unusual that nobody could have imagined, that the Old Town would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be shelled. At that moment, it had a shocking effect, not only on me but on the entire population of Dubrovnik, as far as I was able to learn from speaking to people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber a while back that you would visit your mother once or twice a week in the Old Town. Did you see damage to the Old Town as a result of shelling on your visits to your mother in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the damage you saw to the Old Town from shelling in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Since we came down into Dubrovnik through the high street called Stradun, that was the main street, we would then turn off into side streets such as the Od Puca Street in order to avoid sniper shots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which street is Od Puca, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Od Puca Street. That street is parallel to the main street, Placa, south of Placa, or rather Stradun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about damage? What damage did you see in the Old Town from shelling in October 1991 when you walked through Stradun and Od Puca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the details, but I remember my overall impression. We saw debris after the shelling on Stradun. We saw entire chips that had fallen off roofs, tiles, pieces of roofing. I believe particularly badly hit was Boskovic Street where you could see a lot of so-called stone plastic bits of window frames, some lining from under the roof, and pieces of facade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Stradun itself? Did you see any damage to the paving on the Stradun?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to November 1991, did you see any damage from shelling in November 1991 to the Old Town when you went there to visit your mother?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I will have to be completely honest and tell you that I didn't keep a diary recording what I saw and where I saw it. And too much time has elapsed for me to remember now the details. I cannot tell you anything about the intensity of the shelling on each particular day. But my general impression is that before the 6th, there was much less damage than after the 6th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to the 6th of December, where were you on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th December, I was at home in Lapad. My address is Put Ive Vojnovica 104.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did the shelling start?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Early in the morning. I believe around 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, we were unable to leave our homes. We couldn't go as usual to our office, which was 400 metres away from my apartment. We all went down into shelters, all the residents of our apartment block. And we waited to hear some information on the radio as to what was actually going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your -- was the area in which you were living shelled?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the shelling go on for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It seemed to me that it went on incessantly from 6.00 a.m. Or thereabouts until late afternoon, 5.00 or 6.00 p.m. It seemed to be continuous with a very short break around noon, I believe. I'm not 100 per cent sure any more. But I believe that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your mother in the Old Town on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you contact her that day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the Old Town on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, in the evening, yes, late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it dark?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pitch dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you enter through the Pile gate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I went across Stradun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What I saw was an inferno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean you saw houses on fire or fire or burning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw fire coming out of the houses right at the beginning of Stradun. I believe one was the building of festivals and summer games, and the adjacent buildings around it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the state of Stradun that night?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it in a hellish image. Fire, smoke, debris, you could hardly walk across Stradun. And there were people who were trying to put out the fire. That was the main thing that struck you as you watched, and a lot of commotion. That's all I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from Stradun, did you go to any other places in the Old Town on the evening of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I only went up to the area in front of the St. Blaise Church. I tried to reach the home of my mother, but from some point onwards, I didn't feel safe any more. I couldn't know what would fall on my head as I continued down the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you return home?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return to the Old Town on the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was actually my first real visit when I was able to see clearly what had happened, sometime around 11.00 a.m. I went on foot from Lapad towards downtown. I saw a lot of people coming into the downtown area, silent, mute with tears in their eyes. It's a sight that I will never forget.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you again enter the Old Town through the Pile gate on to Stradun?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described seeing fire, smoke, and debris, and hardly being able to walk across the Stradun when you went there the evening before. What was the state of the Stradun, just the paving, the pavement area, as you walked along Stradun on the morning of the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Fires didn't burn any more, but there was smoke coming out of burnt-down houses at the very beginning of Stradun that I mentioned. I saw the debris that had come out of the window and doors of houses into the street. And I saw the hoses of the firefighters and the remnants of certain parts of burnt-down buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the debris like on the footpaths or the pavement of Stradun? I want you to describe the depth and what you saw on the -- on the Stradun.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was actually a pile of burnt debris, ground, stone, glass, and burnt woodwork from houses, pieces of roofing and doors. A huge amount of debris that made it impossible to walk through, although the first interventions had already started late that evening and continued in the morning, and some part of the way was cleared by the time I returned in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about damage to the buildings on either side of the Stradun? What did you see on the first day you went -- sorry, on the first day you went back, the 7th of December? This is before you conducted your inspections.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The situation was shocking. I did not pay attention to details. Such was the impact of the overall picture of the destroyed town on me. I was unable to concentrate on one building in particular. The overall impression of the burnt town was such that I felt at that moment as if everything had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you what you saw on the morning of the 7th, that is, the damage to buildings on the Stradun and the debris you saw in the streets, compare to damage you had seen in the Old Town in October and November from shelling? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There's no comparison. First of all, there was no fire. There was a huge difference in the quantity of destroyed material. That is the main difference in terms of consequences of shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about holes in the roofs of buildings? Did you see -- On that first day, did you notice or were you looking for holes in roofs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, standing in Stradun and walking up to Knezev Dvor and my mother's home when I wanted to see what her house looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any roof damage, that is, holes in roofs, on the first day you went there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this question. This question was asked only a minute ago and answered. The question on the damage to roofs on the first day. My learned friend, it's page 16, lines 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not sure it was answered. He answered about going to his mother's to see what the house looked like. He didn't answer specifically the question about holes in roofs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Re, so perhaps you better tidy up. The question was asked, Mr. Petrovic, but it was never answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand, Mr. Vukovic? The question was: Did you see on that first day any holes in roofs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw damage to the cathedral on the dome because that's what you could see standing in Stradun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned the Knezev Dvor. Is that in English the rector's palace? I'm sorry, that may sound like an odd question. It is, in fact, the rector's palace. I'll move on. As you came through the city gates, the Pile gates, what did you notice about the walkways, the walls, and the gates in relation to the shelling the night before, or the day before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I have already said what I saw. There was a pile of debris, pieces of material in a much larger quantity incomparable to what was visible in the previous two months, October and November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where had the debris that you saw coming into the Old Town, that is, through the gates near the walkways, city walls, come from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: One could assume the debris had fallen from the roof, from the interior of burnt buildings. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had been the practice in the Old Town in relation to the clearing of debris from the streets after the previous shellings in October and November?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What needed to be done was to clear walkways and roads to be able to pass through by car and on foot, and people did that. People would move the debris aside, clear it -- clear the way so that one can pass through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how soon after the shelling was the debris cleared from the streets in October and November, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. But I believe the reaction was instantaneous. And certain shops windows and even roofs were repaired within a very short time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described going along the Stradun to the cathedral and seeing damage to the dome of the cathedral on the 7th of December. Where else in the Old Town did you go on that morning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I said I went to Buniceva Poljana where my mother's house stands. I saw there something that shocked me concerning the life of my mother. She used to go to the ground floor of the building because that's where she felt safe, as safe as she could be. But on that day, she didn't go to the ground floor. She was on one of the intermediate floors. And then a shell fell on Buniceva Poljana, and the shrapnel completely destroyed the very solid door of that house. So if she had been on the ground floor, she probably wouldn't be alive today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know a shell fell on Buniceva Poljana? What did you see which led you to conclude that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the traces of impact of the shell on the pavement and on the facade of the building which I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the damage you saw on the facade of that building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I could see the traces of impact of what I suppose was shrapnel. We called them dents in the facade or piketina [phoen] in our jargon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a stone building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the trace of the impact of the shell on the pavement that you saw?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We could see the place where the shell fell. It was a depression in the pavement with sharp edges. And in a radiating pattern like when you let a drop fall on a stain of ink, you could see the same pattern on the pavement as a consequence of the impact of the shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this depression, what was the approximate diameter of it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that any more. But it could have been 20 or 30 centimetres of the main depression itself. And if you count the circle around it, it could have been bigger, 2 or 3 metres. And if you also look at the traces on the walls, then you could make it bigger still.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go anywhere else in the Old Town apart from the area where your mother lived and the Stradun on the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I went through the Od Puca Street on the way back. And then I emerged on another street that I don't recall the name of any more. And then I returned to Stradun. I believe it was Siroka Street, and then I returned to Lapad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe the state of Od Puca and Siroka Street as you walked through them that day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Od Puca Street is narrower than Stradun. And my impressions were even more intense. I found a lot of burnt buildings there. Smoke was still coming out of them. And the worst sight was on the corner of Od Puca Street and Siroka Street of which I have a very fond memory of the times from before all that because a painter, Grbic, had a gallery on the ground floor, and he had a wonderful sound studio behind the door. All this was completely destroyed after the 6th, and I was very moved, or rather hard-hit by it. So on my way, I passed through Stradun again and saw again the sight of burnt houses and piles of debris on the pavement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also debris on Od Puca and Siroka Streets?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that debris similar to the debris, the building debris, you described as being on the Stradun?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It all seemed the same to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen a video that Mr. Grbic took which is in evidence here, P66, taken on the 7th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did see some of this footage, and I think that Mr. Grbic's was among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grbic's was the earlier one. That's Exhibit P66. There was also Mr. Jusic's video, and the one we call the JNA video, which is P145.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the three videos, if you accept that Mr. Grbic's was P66 and the earlier one and having viewed it, did that accord with your own recollections of the state of the Old Town on the morning of the 7th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection, Your Honour. First of all, I don't know how the witness can possibly know which exhibit is which one in terms of their numbers, as admitted by this Trial Chamber. That is one objection. P66, secondly, is not Grbic's footage at all. Please look at this particular exhibit before the Honourable Trial Chamber. This is not Grbic's footage. It is footage that was obtained by Grbic and provided by Grbic, but he did not author it in any way. So please, let us not confuse the witness by saying that this is Grbic's footage because no such thing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. exists. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, the question of whether the witness can identify the particular exhibit is a live one which you'll need to work on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, in conferring with the Prosecution lawyers, did we show you three videos?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they described to you as, colloquially, "the Grbic video," that is, a video provided by Mr. Grbic. For the purposes of the record P66. Secondly, a video provided by Mr. Jusic. For the purposes of the record P78. And thirdly a video taken when the JNA were videoing the Old Town on the 8th of December, for the record P145?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of the names of some of the video footage, and I cannot say anything about who was the author of particular footage. But I know that it is under these headings or names that the videos were shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I may deal with this a little later by showing the witness a clip of P66 to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Another possibility might be to have the witness view something with the court officer during the break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, what did you do professionally in the days following the 7th of December and your walk through the Old Town and seeing the damage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My professional activity, as I already said, until the 6th was aimed at taking care of the material that we had in our office. And that was my only activity. After the shelling, since we were in a state of shock, I, myself, called my colleagues at the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, and quite simply I said that we were there, available, to help them in the work that they had already started in terms of identifying the damage that was caused by the shelling. With our colleague Matko Vetma who is a personal friend and colleague, another architect, I spoke to a few colleagues from the town planning office, and I promised them that I would come to their office and help have this identified as quickly as possible, in order to be able to organise help in redressing the damage and repairing it. So at that point in time, that is what I was focussed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had the work in assessing or identifying the damage started before the 6th of December shelling?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Information was compiled about the damage sustained. At that moment, when speaking to my colleagues, I found out about this. I did not have any insight into the actual documentation. It is only later that I found out that they had compiled some papers where they actually identified that damage as well. This was shown on the map, and the actual places were identified by numbers. And also, the degree of damage was shown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was doing this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This was done by colleagues from the institute for the protection of cultural monuments. This was done strictly within their line of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it relate to the damage in October and November to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about UNESCO? Was UNESCO involved in that earlier damage report in October and November?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes. It is only later when I came to the institute that I met two gentlemen, Mr. Bruno Karneze and Colin Kaiser. They were representing UNESCO in Dubrovnik. And as far as I knew then, they had already worked together with our colleagues from the institute for the protection of cultural monuments. They worked on the identification of actual damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying you first met Mr. Karneze and Mr. Kaiser after the 6th of December in the institute office?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the planning to map the damage of the Old Town of Dubrovnik proceed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that unfortunately cataclysm is an integral part of life in Dubrovnik. Earthquakes compelled us to work out a methodology of our own. First of all, in order to protect cultural heritage, and secondly, a methodology to identify the state of the monuments themselves. I am not a conservation expert, but through my activity I did learn that after the earthquake of 1979, when Dubrovnik was affected by a bad earthquake, a particular methodology had been evolved in order to identify damage as soon as possible. And zoning was carried out in this respect. That is to say, various sectors within the nucleus of the Old Town. So that was one matter. Another matter was identifying the degree of damage sustained by particular buildings or sections. And there were different categories involved depending on the degree and type of damage sustained. This was used in the first moment in order to establish a pattern which then made it possible to identify what the situation was within the Old Town nucleus. This actually has to do with your question related to planning. And if you wish, this is direct experience I had while working on town planning myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the people who devised the plan to map the damage of the Old Town from the shelling of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that my colleagues at the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments had this methodology. It had been evolved already in 1979 due to the damage sustained then, and it was worked on further. It was supplemented by ways of establishing damage caused by shelling. So it is the result of a synthesis of the previous methodology and the new situation caused by the shelling itself. As for the persons involved, this is the institution for the protection of cultural monuments. According to the information I had, and I did not directly take part in this, the gentlemen from UNESCO participated in this effort as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the division of Dubrovnik into zones for mapping following the earthquake in 1979. How many zones was the Old Town divided into?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many zones, but I think it's around 17 or something like that, or around 20. Between 15 or 20 approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned categories of damage. Were they the four categories of damage which are referred to in the institute report, which is P51/ID?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, these are four basic categories in view of the degree of damage sustained by an individual building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who devised those four categories?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But having talked to my colleagues from the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, the assumption is that it was the result of a team effort. I cannot tell you who all the participants were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you physically go about inspecting the damage to the buildings and objects in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, I have to say that when we came to the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, we were given some preliminary information that our colleagues had had before our arrival, before we from the town planning office arrived and people from architectural bureaus and other people who took part. So we received this preliminary information about the effects caused by individual projectiles when impacting. I remember well that we worked in a room that was like an anteroom, leading into the institute itself, and there were maps of the entire municipality on the wall. There were maps of the Old Town nucleus as well, and within all of that there was a board where the type of projectiles, the types of projectiles were depicted. And the effects of these projectiles were shown. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So this was this preliminary information that we did not hear about directly, but the people from the institute said that they received this information from the civil defence. And we talked to our colleagues from the institute about this, and this is something that prepared us for the identification that we were involved in later. So how do we go about doing this? On the basis of this preliminary information --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just ask you to pause. I'll go back to what you just mentioned. What was the purpose of your being asked to identify from that board the projectiles and the damage that they caused?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, this was not of decisive importance in terms of the assessment that we were supposed to carry out. It just meant whether by the nature of the effect it caused it led to the kind of damage that required total restoration of a building. For example, if a building had burned down, then it had to be reconstructed totally. On the other hand, we had some projectiles that affected the surface only, damaging the walls or roof only. And there was the so-called indirect effect from shrapnel when adjacent buildings were hit and others were indirectly affected. So that was the point of this identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the information you were given about the types of projectiles that you might find or might have caused damage to buildings and objects in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were made aware of three or four types of projectiles, I believe, that were used in the area, at least that's the information we received. So we were talking about mortar shells, 120 millimetres, then mortar shells of 80 or 82 millimetres, I believe. Then there were the so-called Maljutkas. These were guided missiles. And I think there were tank shells or cannon shells. I cannot remember exactly now, but it was something along those lines more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What experience had you had, if any, in ballistics' identification before seeing this information on the board in the institute office?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, I didn't have any such experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that based upon the information which was on that board that you would be able to competently identify the cause of, or the type of projectile which may have hit a building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to a large extent, yes. Not 100 per cent, but as much as we needed at that point in time. As I said, the point of our identification was to ascertain the actual damage sustained. It wasn't to be used as any kind of evidence or whatever. We wanted to embark on the restoration and reconstruction of buildings as soon as possible. So that was relevant for the problems we were facing at the time. As for the rest, we could not imagine that any such thing would come out of it, and we did not even receive any instructions as to how we should proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to what you did, what did you do based upon that preliminary information? How were you divided and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the organisation of the people who were engaged in this effort involved the following: We were divided into teams of two or three, and everybody got a particular block. This had to do with the zoning that we've already discussed. So we simply went out into the area rather systematically, from one house to the other, from one door to the other, from one floor to the other. We looked at it all systematically, and it consisted of first identifying the problem visually, and then the second level was compiling information, interviewing persons who were either in the building itself or near the building. And of course, the preliminary information that we had in terms of the sources, that is to say, the type of impact and so on. So that was the approach we had in this identification effort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the composition of the teams? How were they divided up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we did not have much leeway. We did not have a lot of people to work with. We were all in a state of shock, and we wanted to identify the damage as soon as possible. So the teams mainly consisted of people who were either architectural technicians or who were architects, so there would be one or two or three of them, sometimes even four persons. At any rate, the teams were small. And they had some foreknowledge, so to speak, but it was perhaps at a lower professional level, but quite sufficient for this type of identification that we were after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, do you think, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What we'll do now is have the first morning break now. We've gone for an hour and a half. And we'll continue with the evidence after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Vukovic, you were telling the Trial Chamber about the teams of people who were architectural technicians or architects, two or three or four, who were going around inspecting the city, the Old Town, block by block. Who was on your team?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a permanent team so that Mr. Vetma inspected some buildings, then my colleague Mrs. Davorka Kunic, and another colleague, Mrs. Peko, plus Mrs. Karaman. That is the team of people with whom I went out to carry out inspections and evaluations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mrs. Peko, you referred to, that's Mrs. Lucijana Peko. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're saying you did your inspections in a combination of those various people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of map were -- was the institute using of the Old Town? What was on the map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We used the as-built plan of the entire town with our coded blocks, sections indicated, and specific streets inside sections, and that's the plan we used when carrying out inspections. Each team was assigned one section and the plan for that section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a bundle of documents which contain 18 separate maps and an overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown this document. For the information of the Trial Chamber, these are extracts from P51/ID which are all the maps relating to each zone but together in one bundle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, you see on the first page, it's an overview map. Is that an overview map of Dubrovnik, of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is divided into 17 separate zones?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are the documents following each -- a larger map of each of the 17 zones marked on the front page?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the addition on the second page of one with a Z, a large handwritten Z on it, which is my marking. Does the second page refer to -- the second page relate to the city walls and walkways?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it -- were these the documents that you used, that the institute and you used in dividing the work between teams and assigning sectors or zones for each team to inspect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May these be received into evidence as one bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, the second page of this document is, indeed, a graphic depiction of the entire Old Town, but this page does not reflect what my learned friend indicated. It reflects alleged hits on the walls of the Old Town. Therefore, my learned friend did not present the contents of this second page in a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. proper way. And we do not see on what basis it can be tendered. The other pages contain maps, however, and we do not object that they be offered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... to be Exhibit P68 already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In fact, it is. I put it in only so that the Trial Chamber can see that it relates only to the walkways. It is not tendered at the moment on the basis that that's where the hits actually were, but only on the basis that that was the map that the institute was using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you purporting to tender the whole bundle or simply the first two pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The whole bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, are you going to tell us more about what's in the bundle through the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it that they're tendered merely as a more detailed plan of each section that's set out on the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's all you're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's only for convenience as to how the city was divided up, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no damage depicted on or purported to be depicted on any of those maps bar the first one which is only put there to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not the first one. The second.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, the second one. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that is already an exhibit through Dr. Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In those circumstances, I think the whole bundle should be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit is P172.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What instructions were given, Mr. Vukovic, to the teams as to how to assess the damage, apart from what you described about -- about describing projectiles?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I already said in the introductory part that our methodology of evaluation was based on identifying damage to construction; that is to say, the degree of damage to construction after impact of projectiles. That was the first stage of identification. We had to establish whether the building was completely destroyed by the hit. In the second stage, we had to evaluate whether the walls and roof were damaged. That was the second category. The third category was one of the two, either the roof or the walls. And the fourth category were buildings that were indirectly damaged by shrapnel from projectiles that hit the adjacent building. This was followed by an evaluation of the degree of damage. Apart from that, we had to establish the source of damage, to find out what damaged the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the teams instructed to record their observations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We had a form to fill in which contained the code of the building that was to be observed. And based on that form, we would fill in the time of inspection. Second, the name of the owner, if that was possible to identify, if the owner was present. The third item was description. We filled that in based on our observations and comments from neighbours or tenants. We wrote in hand using these two main sources of information. We did that on so-called field drawings. And the markings would be then drawn into our own plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the code of the building. What are you referring to when you say "code"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. Could you clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Your answer was "we had a form to fill in which contained the code of the building that was to be observed." What did you mean when you said "code"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Code may be a pretentious term. It was a mark of that particular building within a block of buildings. That facilitated our work in identifying the building and systematising the data once we were back in our office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean by that that if you located damage on a building in, say, zone 8, you gave it a number, 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on? So it became 8-1, 8-2, 8-3, 8-4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blocks were marked by Roman numbers. And inside blocks, there was a mark in Arabic numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these marks in Arabic numbers, that's 1, 2, 3, 4, et cetera, bear any relationship to the street number or the cadastre number?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they chosen purely for the purposes of the report noting the damage to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think this material was used only for this report, but I don't know whether it was used before or after for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave the -- who was responsible for allocating numbers, like Roman numeral VIII-1, 2, 3, 4, and so on, for each block?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that with any certainty. But I suppose that this system was established before, after the 1979 earthquake. Already at that time, we had as-built plans that used these indications. I don't know how long ago it dates back to, but in any case I had this system, these plans, when I was drawing up my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the system. But who was responsible at the end of the day for allocating the individual damage numbers within a block? That is, 1, 2, 3, 4 sequentially. Who did that once the questionnaire was brought back?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, you want me to tell you who was responsible for assigning a particular block of buildings to a particular team?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Who was responsible for putting the numbers relating to the damage on a building that had been assessed as damaged?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was our colleagues from the Institute for the Protection and Conservation of Cultural Monuments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were buildings in which no damage was assessed, were they given numbers or were they left blank?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. All the buildings were marked, and I suppose this system was used -- had been used since the time of the earthquake in 1979.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the same form given to all the teams that went to all of the zones?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly any more, but I believe every team certainly got an excerpt from the hall reflecting the part of town or the blocks that were assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start your physical inspections of buildings in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime between the 10th and the 12th, or maybe 13th. I cannot recall precisely any more. I believe it must be indicated somewhere in these documents, but it was immediately after the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you take with you in your inspections?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I had a notepad and a file with writing paper and a plan of the block of buildings we were supposed to inspect marked with numbers. We also had about a dozen of these forms to fill in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which zones were you allocated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, I was assigned zone 8, or rather a part of it; then zone 9. In fact, when I say "zone," I mean block. 9, 10, and 11, if memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already mentioned some of the details of how you carried out your inspections. Going to the blocks which you inspected, did you go to every building and structure within that zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go to every building or structure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Because when we looked from very narrow streets, we could not ascertain whether there was any damage or not. The only way to establish whether a building was hit was to go into it and inspect it from bottom to top. In that way, we had sufficiently good control over the whole area of the building and could establish what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How thorough were your inspections of each of the buildings you went into?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to take into account that our inspection was a preliminary one. Within a relatively short time, we had to make complete assessments covering all the buildings that were damaged, and the very term "preliminary" means that more detailed evaluations were to follow. To establish the degree of damage and those later evaluations, more complete ones, would eventually form the basis for restoration works. Therefore, our observations were only preliminary, of informative nature, and sufficient for that level of evaluation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the average length of time you spent examining each building or structure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From the document that we produced, you can see that, because we also noted the time spent in each building. It would be 20 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of impression could you gain in 20 to 30 minutes in the building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was enough to identify what we were supposed to identify at that moment; that is, the degree of damage and the source of damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to gain access to every building within the blocks or zones that you inspected? Sorry, that you were allocated.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. We entered all the buildings that were possible to enter. However, there were buildings that were completely burnt down where you couldn't get any further from the entrance or the ground floor, that were completely destroyed. And in all buildings that were not destroyed, we inspected literally every nook and cranny.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any safety issues relating to human habitation or occupation of the structures you examined?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand this question. Do you mean the safety of us who did the question or safety in terms of the fitness of that building for residential purposes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was mainly directing it at the occupation. But could you also please answer your own personal safety in terms of -- in your inspection of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that there was a degree of danger involved in our work because we didn't know whether the shelling would start again or not. However, we went into it enthusiastically following our main objective, to assess the damage. Renewed shelling was always a possibility, but fortunately it didn't happen. Second, in our notes, we indicated all buildings which continued to be fit for occupation, wherever it was possible to establish. We would also write that down certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a practice in relation to the allocation of blocks or zones every day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, we had the task to cover a certain block. Every morning, we would report to our head office, which was in the building of the Institute for the Protection of Monuments. It was a big room with drawing boards and boards on the walls. We would have a meeting there before going out into the field. We would make a plan, a practical plan, how we would go about it. And then we would go to work. After the inspection was completed, we would go back to the office to systematise the results of the inspection and prepare a summary of our findings for each block.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on the handwritten annotations you made on the form that every team had?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We did everything in hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Mr. Kaiser -- sorry, Dr. Kaiser and Mr. Karneze participated in these morning briefings or meetings before people went out to inspect the buildings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I used to see them. They were with us occasionally. I personally talked to Mr. Karneze and Mr. Colin Kaiser. And we established a rather close contact based on our common professional interest. As far as I can recollect, they were not there every day, at least not every time when I attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The forms that you were filling in had an entry on them for filling in the date of the damage.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The date and time when we arrived would be marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How or what did you do to assess, what inquiries or what did you do to assess when the building was damaged when you inspected buildings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that every resident knew very well what happened to his own house and in the immediate vicinity. So our evaluations of impacts were based on information provided by the tenants or neighbours and from what we could see with our own eyes, burnt beams, woodwork, pieces of stone that had fallen off as a result of impacts, et cetera. Every shell that fell on Dubrovnik first hit the hearts of our people before exploding, so they knew very well what exactly was done and how.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you fill in the -- or did you put on each form relating to each building you inspected a date under the heading "date of incident"; that is, the date of the impact or damage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the evaluated, the assessed date of impact?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On each of the forms, there's a date and hour of inspection. That's the time when you inspected the building. Underneath that, it says "date of incident." On each of the buildings you inspected, did you fill in a date for when you believed the building was damaged?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think for the most part, yes. As far as most buildings are concerned. I told you already that our inspection was preliminary. We were supposed to gather all available information. And at that moment, it didn't matter to us so much whether it was damaged on the 6th or before; what mattered was to establish the degree of damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago your evaluation was based upon what people were -- was partly based upon what people were telling you. Were there instances where you were told that the building had been damaged both on December the 6th and either in October or November 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the information you brought back on the forms every day collated into the final or the preliminary report, which is a typed document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not there in the final stage of the elaboration of the document in terms of the actual typing and the final version. This was done by my colleagues at the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments. But the text was worked on and the visual images were, too, so I did not have much insight into the completion of this documentation, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the typed version of the forms which you submitted after inspecting buildings in December 1991? That is, have you looked at the -- how your work appears in the preliminary report as published?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did look at that. But not with the intention of checking out to see whether somebody had changed the findings in any way. I was just interested in what the material actually looked like. This was the final version when we could see the integral material and when we could familiarise ourselves with what had been written, and then we could intervene in terms of whether any mistakes had been made or not. As far as I can remember, I had no objections whatsoever in respect of my own part that I looked at and that had been processed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you are concerned, are you satisfied that what is in the report under your name, that is, the buildings under your name that you inspected, accurately reflects your observations that you recorded?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, there was no great possibility of deviation. It could be established immediately whether this was actually the material I had work on. I was indeed very pleased with the way in which this had been done in terms of the final presentation, the graphic part, the text, and the material as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also referred to a graphic part. Are you referring to diagrams, maps, photographs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean maps first and foremost. So that is a graphic depiction of the blocks where we exactly registered a certain type of damage. The impact that caused the damage, and I think the third map showed the category of damage sustained. Also, there were photographs which in a way provided supplementary documentation for the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took the photographs which accompany the text of the buildings you examined?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was actually done by Mr. Milenko Mojas, an employee of the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments. He's a professional photographer actually, and he has had many years of experience with this kind of work, together with a colleague of his who is not from the institute but who is a journalist, rather, a photographer, a journalist. He actually took these photographs on the basis of the information that we compiled for a particular block, but then he also relied on his own concept of photography. For some important buildings he went and he took more photographs and completed the documentation in this way. I would like to point out that there were only two men, or rather there was only one man. And physically, it was not possible for him to be everywhere no matter how hard he tried to do his best. But anyway, we could put these photographs into our completed report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mojas ever accompany you when you were doing your inspections?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing him in the Old Town taking photographs at the time when you were doing your inspections?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him several times. I also saw him at the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, and that is where we discussed how what we had inspected should be presented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include adding his photographs to the various buildings inspected and detailed in the report? When I say "adding," I mean selecting photographs to include in the report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a compilation of the buildings which bear your name within the report, the preliminary report, which is P51/ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown a copy of the compilation and an index to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go into the details of the extract from the larger report, I'll turn to something else. Did you bring with you to The Hague, Mr. Vukovic, a large overhead photograph of the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I would ask you kindly, if possible, to show it to the Honourable Trial Chamber. It was taken in May 2001. It's an aerial image of the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took the photograph or where did you get the photograph from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That photograph was borrowed from the Institute for Reconstruction. So that is an institution that works on operational reconstruction of the town established as far back as 1979 after the earthquake. So they're in charge of reconstructing and repairing the town after the shelling, too. Geofoto is the organisation that actually took the photograph. They are a professional organisation that is engaged in this line of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it show an aerial view of the Old Town as reconstructed by May 2001?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the situation in the month of May when everything had been taken care of in a way, so this is a good opportunity for you to see what it was like at the time and what was actually the object of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does this photograph show an overview of all the locations, an aerial overview of all the locations that you inspected in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is an overview of the entire town, including the locations that I inspected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, in their repaired state almost ten years later?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said yes, Mr. Vukovic, but no answer is recorded.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the photograph please be distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, I think you have the original photograph there from which we've made copies.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
